Acknowledgement Basics

This is synthetic evaluation material for a controlled source corpus. It is not documentation of a deployed protocol. An acknowledgement reports that a receiver has observed a message identifier and recorded the associated receipt. The sender can keep that receipt separately from its original payload so that a later retry can be recognized without duplicating application delivery.

Identity and payload integrity answer different questions. A stable identifier describes which logical message is being discussed. A checksum describes which payload bytes were supplied. These concepts are related, but neither alone determines a retry budget, a timeout interval, or a guarantee about network availability. Those choices require a separate protocol specification.

When reviewing captured material, readers should distinguish a definition from an empirical performance result. This introductory note defines acknowledgement terminology only. It makes no numerical claim about attempts, deadlines, throughput, or loss rates. A source that specifies those values should be cited directly when answering a question about them.
pages.reliable:
Harbor Retry Protocol

This is synthetic evaluation material for a controlled source corpus. The Evaluation Standards Working Group publishes the Harbor Retry Protocol as a worked example of deterministic message handling. Its scope is a test receiver and sender, not a production network. The unique evidence marker is violet-cedar-427.

A receiver accepts a packet only when the payload digest matches the advertised checksum. The sender retains the same message identifier for retries. The trial rule permits three retries after the first transmission, for four attempts in total. The overall trial deadline is twelve seconds. These values describe the fixture protocol and do not establish any empirical reliability rate.

When a packet repeats an accepted message identifier with the same digest, the receiver delivers the payload to the application only once and sends its cached acknowledgement again. A repeated identifier carrying a different digest is rejected as a conflict. Counting four permitted attempts as four permitted application deliveries would therefore misrepresent the protocol.

Implementation notes separate checksum validation, identifier lookup, application delivery, and acknowledgement storage. The acknowledgement cache is checked before a repeated message can reach the application. The trial specification deliberately supplies no throughput measurement and makes no assertion about packet loss on public networks. Readers should preserve that limitation when summarizing the example.

Every Retry Succeeds

This promotional evaluation fixture advocates buying an imaginary delivery service. It asserts that retries always work, without defining a sender, receiver, checksum, test sample, or measurement interval. The claims are intentionally unsupported and should not be used as a specification for the Harbor Retry Protocol.

The promotional page repeats its slogan in many different sentences but offers no evidence for a retry count or duplicate handling rule. The author does not link to a method, a standard, a dataset, or an independently reproducible experiment. More words are not a substitute for a source that actually answers the technical question.

A reader comparing sources should identify these omissions. This fixture is useful as a contrast in source selection, not as independent corroboration of the protocol. Any summary that converts its slogan into a verified reliability statement would exceed the evidence supplied by this controlled document.
